extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; readers interested in early American political press
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes evaluative principles and practical standards for early American newspapers and political journalism as discussed in a history-of-journalism textbook chapter covering the post-Revolution/early Republic period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ardent advocacy of the Federal constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy journalism that strongly champions a political cause — e.g., 'It was such ardent advocacy of the Federal constitution... that brought to the Federal party its main support.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasive, sustained advocacy (backed by reasoned essays like the Federalist) can mobilize political support and shape party formation; effective advocacy may require coordination with influential writers and repeated publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing public laws gratuitously (public service vs. profit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing official public laws without charge as an expression of loyalty and public service (illustrated by Major Russell printing the public laws gratis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such acts can demonstrate civic commitment and earn reputational reward (e.g., Washington insisted a payment be made as a 'debt of honor'). This is a model of service-oriented journalism rather than purely commercial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and commercial viability (daily publication in response to advertisements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitioning a paper to daily publication due to increased advertisement volume — e.g., the Pennsylvania Packet became a daily 'evidently in response to a large increase in the advertisements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication frequency should match demand and revenue models; substantial advertising can justify and sustain more frequent (daily) issues even if editorial content is limited at first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting and paper tone ('gentlemen's paper' vs. 'mechanics')
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing a paper's tone and content to a target audience: the Gazette of the United States described itself to both 'people of wealth and culture' and to 'mechanics' (the 'plain people').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mismatch between high-toned content and the intended audience reduces appeal; prospectuses often explicitly state intended readership and tailor content (debates, essays, news) accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing debates and important papers; serious thoughtful articles on government
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper's role as an organ for government and political thought: 'it would print the debates and the important papers; it would contain from time to time serious and thoughtful articles on government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including primary documents (debates, official papers) and substantial commentary establishes a paper's authority and civic function; this is especially expected of 'national' or 'gentlemen's' organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan alignment and functioning as a party organ
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers operating as explicit organs of political parties or factions (e.g., Federalist and anti-Federalist organs, papers 'defend[ing] the Federal party' or serving as the 'first Democratic organ').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organized, partisan presses coordinate messaging (essays, replies, ridicules) and are often financed or supported by party figures; producers should expect both political influence and partisan backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinated reply/organ strategy (need for a combatant organ)
rubrics_metrics.description: The strategic necessity of creating or supporting a paper to reply to opposition — Jefferson and allies sought an active combatant in the newspaper field and organized Freneau/the National Gazette for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political actors should cultivate or fund newspapers to provide systematic rebuttals and sustained replies to adversary publications; concentration and coordination amplify impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial backing, patronage, and editorial survival
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependence of papers on financial support, loans, patronage, or government positions (e.g., Fenno's appeals for loans, Hamilton/Rufus King raising funds, Jefferson arranging subscriptions and positions for allies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic viability often requires patronage or private financing; editors may accept government appointments or party support to sustain publication — but such ties influence editorial independence and alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary ability and quality of writing as influence (examples: The Federalist, essays)
rubrics_metrics.description: High literary and argumentative quality (Hamilton, Madison, Jay's Federalist; Dickinson's 'Farmers' Letters') establishes credibility and can decisively influence public acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-crafted essays and superior prose enhance persuasive power and longevity; quality writing can lift journalism from ephemeral to foundational political literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ridicule and personal attack as a risky tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule and personal mockery in commentary (Greenleaf's ridicule of a pageant) can provoke violent backlash (mob attack, destruction of press).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While ridicule can mobilize or inflame opinion, it risks provoking physical retaliation and may endanger the paper's operations; editors should weigh provocation against safety and strategic goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as engine of public opinion and guardian of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that freedom and security of the press depend on 'public opinion, and on the general spirit of the people and the government' and that newspapers are the 'most effectual engines' to inform and mobilize the populace (Jefferson's views).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press producers should aim to inform broadly and penetrate the mass of the people; the health of public opinion is the ultimate safeguard for press freedoms — reach and accessibility are therefore strategic priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing advertisements and editorial content
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial realities: a paper may contain 'plenty of advertisements but not a single line of comment' initially (as with the first daily issue of the Pennsylvania Packet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must balance revenue-generating advertisements with editorial content; the initial commercial makeup of issues can reflect business strategy even when editorial ambition exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial consistency and loyalty through party changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors maintaining party loyalty over time, even as issues shift (Russell remained a Federalist up through Madison's administration despite changing party fortunes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency can cement reputation and readership among a faction but may reduce broader appeal when political winds change; loyalty often aligns with patronage and editorial stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical editorial tactics: printing series and regular numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing sustained series and regular numbers (e.g., the Federalist essays appearing 'several numbers... every week' and being copied by friendly papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, serialized publication of essays or argumentative series increases dissemination and allows allied papers to amplify messages; scheduling and syndication are important production tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' personal risk and forms of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors frequently faced personal danger and varied forms of punishment (e.g., attack, horse-whipping) as a consequence of partisan journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should be aware of the potential for physical or social reprisals; historical context shapes the level of risk and expected reprisals for provocative journalism.
